subject: maths
title: Chapter 9 · Test 1
summary: Chapter 9 test 1: 15 questions on sampling, box plots, standard deviation, scatterplots, time series and evaluating statistical reports.
body: This test covers Chapter 9 · Statistics: collecting data and sampling, box plots and the five-number summary, standard deviation, scatterplots and lines of best fit, time-series data and evaluating statistical reports. It has 15 multiple-choice questions, from easy to challenge. Allow about 25 minutes and work with no notes. A calculator is allowed for this test, but show your working on paper so you can check each step. Many questions use a graph or diagram — read the axes and scales carefully before you answer.

questions.prompt: A teacher uses an alphabetical class list, picks a random starting name, then chooses every 12th name after it. What type of sample is this?
questions.explanation: A random start followed by every 12th name is a systematic sample. It is not stratified, because the list was not split into groups.
steps: Look at the rule: a random start, then every 12th name on one list.
That is the definition of a systematic sample.

mistakes.B: Step 1: a stratified sample splits the list into groups first. Here one list is stepped through every 12th name.
mistakes.C: Step 1: the students did not volunteer — the teacher chose them by a rule.
mistakes.D: Step 1: a census uses every student, but only every 12th student is chosen.

questions.topic: Box plots and the five-number summary
questions.prompt: The box plot shows the minutes a group of students spent on homework one night. What is the upper quartile (Q3)?
questions.explanation: Q3 is the right-hand end of the box: 25 minutes. 33 is the maximum, at the end of the whisker.
steps: The box runs from Q1 to Q3.
Its right-hand end is at 25, so Q3 = 25 minutes.

mistakes.A: Step 1: 19 is the line inside the box, the median. Q3 is the right end of the box.
mistakes.C: Step 1: 33 is the end of the right whisker, the maximum. Q3 is the right end of the box.
mistakes.D: Step 1: 14 is the left end of the box, Q1. Q3 is the right end.

questions.diagram_alt: A box plot of homework minutes on a scale from 5 to 35: minimum 8, Q1 14, median 19, Q3 25, maximum 33

questions.topic: Scatterplots and lines of best fit
questions.prompt: The scatterplot shows the height and arm span of 12 people. Which best describes the relationship?
questions.explanation: The dots rise from left to right (positive) and sit close to a straight line (strong). They do not fall, so it is not negative.
steps: Direction: as height increases, arm span increases — positive.
Strength: the dots are close to a line — strong.

mistakes.A: Step 1: the dots RISE from left to right, so the correlation is positive.
mistakes.B: Step 2: the dots lie very close to a straight line, so it is strong.
mistakes.D: Step 1: there is a clear upward pattern in the dots.

questions.diagram_alt: Scatterplot of arm span against height for 12 people from about 148 to 182 cm; the dots rise in a tight straight-line pattern

questions.prompt: The graph shows a Melbourne household's electricity use each month of one year (J, F, M, … are January, February, March, …). The same pattern happens every year. Which feature does it show?

options.B: Seasonality, with a peak in summer
options.D: Seasonality, with a peak in winter

questions.explanation: Use peaks in June–August (winter, when heating is used) and the pattern repeats every year, so it is seasonal. It is not a summer peak — Australian summer is December to February.
steps: A pattern that repeats every year is seasonality.
The highest values are in June, July and August — winter in Melbourne.

mistakes.A: Step 2: use rises to July, then FALLS again — it is not a steady increase.
mistakes.B: Step 2: the peak is in June–August, which is winter in Melbourne.
mistakes.C: Step 1: the high values build up and fall away over several months, and it repeats every year — that is a seasonal pattern, not one spike.

questions.diagram_alt: Time-series graph of monthly electricity use: 420, 410, 450, 520, 600, 690, 720, 700, 610, 520, 450, 430 kWh from January to December; the vertical axis starts at 300

questions.prompt: A factory has 600 office workers and 400 factory-floor workers. A stratified sample of 50 workers is chosen. How many factory-floor workers should be in it?
questions.explanation: Factory-floor workers are 400 ÷ 1000 = 0.4 of the workforce, and 0.4 × 50 = 20. Splitting 25 and 25 ignores the group sizes.

mistakes.B: Step 2: 50 ÷ 2 = 25 shares the sample equally. The groups are different sizes.
mistakes.C: Step 2: 400 ÷ 50 = 8 divides the wrong numbers. Find 400 ÷ 1000 first.
mistakes.D: Step 2: 30 is the share for the 600 office workers.

questions.topic: Box plots and the five-number summary
questions.prompt: A data set has Q1 = 40 and Q3 = 52. Which of these values is an outlier?
questions.explanation: IQR = 12, so the fences are 40 − 18 = 22 and 52 + 18 = 70. Only 72 is beyond a fence. 70 sits exactly on the fence, so it is not an outlier.
steps: Only 72 is beyond a fence (greater than 70), so 72 is the outlier.

mistakes.A: Step 3: the upper fence is exactly 70. A value must be BEYOND the fence to be an outlier.
mistakes.C: Step 2: 64 = Q3 + IQR. The fence uses 1.5 × IQR, so 64 is inside it.
mistakes.D: Step 3: the lower fence is exactly 22, so 22 is not beyond it.

questions.prompt: Find the population standard deviation of 3, 5, 7, correct to 2 decimal places.
questions.explanation: Mean 5; squared deviations 4, 0, 4 total 8; σ = √(8 ÷ 3) ≈ 1.63. Stopping at 8 ÷ 3 gives the variance.

mistakes.A: Step 3: 8 ÷ 3 ≈ 2.67 is the variance. Take the square root.
mistakes.B: Step 3: √(8 ÷ 2) divides by n − 1. Population σ divides by n = 3.
mistakes.D: Step 2: (2 + 0 + 2) ÷ 3 averages the plain distances. Square each deviation first.

questions.topic: Scatterplots and lines of best fit
questions.prompt: The line of best fit on the scatterplot passes through (0, 15) and (20, 75). Use its equation to predict the distance thrown after 12 hours of training.
questions.explanation: Gradient = (75 − 15) ÷ 20 = 3, so y = 3x + 15 and y = 3 × 12 + 15 = 51 m. Leaving out the intercept gives 36.
steps: Gradient = (75 − 15) ÷ (20 − 0) = 3; the intercept is 15, so y = 3x + 15.

mistakes.B: Step 3: you multiplied the intercept 15 by 12. Use y = 3 × 12 + 15.
mistakes.C: Step 3: 75 m is the line's value at 20 hours. Substitute x = 12.

questions.diagram_alt: Scatterplot of distance thrown against hours of training from 2 to 18 hours, with a line of best fit through the marked points (0, 15) and (20, 75)

questions.prompt: In a group of 7 students, the weekly pocket money is $20, $25, $30, $30, $35, $40 and $1000. Which value should a fair report give as the typical amount?
questions.explanation: The median, $30, is the middle amount and is not affected by the $1000 outlier. The mean, about $168.57, is more than four times what six of the seven students get.
steps: $1000 is an outlier, so use the median for a typical value.
In order, the middle (4th) amount is $30.

mistakes.B: Step 2: one student's $1000 drags the mean far above what the other six get.
mistakes.C: Step 1: the range measures spread, not a typical amount.
mistakes.D: Step 1: $1000 is the outlier, the least typical amount.

questions.topic: Box plots and the five-number summary
questions.prompt: The parallel box plots show the heights of Year 8 and Year 9 students. Which statement is true?

options.A: Year 8 has the larger interquartile range
options.B: About 75% of the Year 9 students are at least as tall as the median Year 8 student
options.C: About half of the Year 9 students are taller than 166 cm
options.D: Every Year 9 student is taller than every Year 8 student

questions.explanation: Year 9's Q1 (153) equals Year 8's median (153), and about 75% of Year 9 is at or above Q1. Year 9's IQR (13) is larger than Year 8's (10).
steps: Year 9's lower quartile is also 153 cm, and about 75% of values are at or above Q1.
So about 75% of Year 9 are at least as tall as the median Year 8 student.

mistakes.A: Step 2: IQR Year 8 = 158 − 148 = 10; Year 9 = 166 − 153 = 13. Year 9's is larger.
mistakes.C: Step 1: 166 is Year 9's Q3, so only about 25% are taller.
mistakes.D: Step 2: the shortest Year 9 student (145 cm) is shorter than many Year 8 students.

questions.diagram_alt: Parallel box plots of height. Year 8: minimum 140, Q1 148, median 153, Q3 158, maximum 170. Year 9: minimum 145, Q1 153, median 160, Q3 166, maximum 178

questions.prompt: In a quiz, 2 students scored 1, 3 students scored 2 and 5 students scored 3. The mean is 2.3. Find the population standard deviation, correct to 2 decimal places.

mistakes.A: Step 3: 6.1 ÷ 10 = 0.61 is the variance. Take the square root.
mistakes.B: Step 3: √(6.1 ÷ 9) divides by n − 1. Population σ divides by 10.
mistakes.D: Step 1: 2.3 is the mean. Find the squared deviations from it.

questions.prompt: A shop sold 14, 20, 17, 23 and 26 bikes in five weeks. What is the SECOND 3-point moving average?
questions.explanation: The second moving average uses weeks 2, 3 and 4: (20 + 17 + 23) ÷ 3 = 20. Using weeks 1–3 gives the first one, 17.
steps: The first average uses weeks 1–3; the second slides along one, to weeks 2–4.

mistakes.A: Step 1: 17 is the FIRST moving average (weeks 1–3). The second uses weeks 2–4.
mistakes.B: Step 2: 60 is the total of weeks 2–4. Divide by 3.
mistakes.C: Step 1: 22 is the THIRD moving average (weeks 3–5). Slide along only one week from the start.

questions.prompt: Support for a council policy fell from 60% to 45% of residents. Which description is correct?

options.A: A fall of 15 percentage points, which is a 25% decrease
options.B: A fall of 15 percentage points, which is a 15% decrease
options.C: A fall of 25 percentage points, which is a 15% decrease
options.D: A fall of 15 percentage points, which is a 33.3% decrease

questions.explanation: The rates differ by 60 − 45 = 15 percentage points, and 15 ÷ 60 × 100 = 25% decrease. Dividing by 45 gives 33.3%, which uses the wrong base.

mistakes.B: Step 2: the percentage decrease compares 15 with the starting 60: 15 ÷ 60.
mistakes.C: Step 1: the difference in the two rates is 60 − 45 = 15 points, not 25.
mistakes.D: Step 2: you divided by the new value, 45. Divide by the starting value, 60.

questions.topic: Scatterplots and lines of best fit
questions.prompt: The line of best fit linking a phone's age x (months) and its battery health y (%) is y = −0.8x + 64. According to the line, at what age is the battery health 40%?
questions.explanation: Set y = 40: 40 = −0.8x + 64, so −0.8x = −24 and x = 30 months. Substituting 40 for x answers a different question.

mistakes.A: Step 1: you substituted 40 for x. Here 40 is the battery health, so set y = 40.
mistakes.C: Step 2: 40 = −0.8x + 64 gives 0.8x = 64 − 40. You added instead of subtracting.
mistakes.D: Step 3: −0.8x = −24, and a negative divided by a negative is positive.

questions.prompt: Researchers catch and band 60 birds on an island, then release them. Later they catch 45 birds, and 9 have bands. Estimate the number of birds on the island.
questions.explanation: In the second catch 9 out of 45 (one fifth) are banded, so the 60 banded birds are about one fifth of all birds: N = 60 × 45 ÷ 9 = 300. Adding the catches (96) only counts birds actually seen.
steps: The banded fraction should match: 9 ÷ 45 = 60 ÷ N.

mistakes.A: Step 1: 60 + 45 − 9 counts only birds that were caught. Use the banded fraction to scale up.
mistakes.B: Step 2: you worked out 60 × 9 ÷ 45. The equation is 9 ÷ 45 = 60 ÷ N, so N = 60 × 45 ÷ 9.
mistakes.D: Step 2: 60 × 45 forgets to divide by the 9 banded birds.
